note: Rounds 1-3 of scripts/workflows/lesson-treatment.js (run wf_30890166-cd3) on series/critic/lessons/treatment-input.json: two critics per round, the average kept, choices under 8 redone.

feedback: 'Starts are always hard.' is plain, true to 屯 and much closer to the intent than the deer line. The drawing is thin: a small comma-shaped bud rises in the dark with no visible ground, so 'pushing up through the earth in three strains' is not seen. The sentence carries this one. A visible ground line for the sprout to break through would make it an 8 or more.

A sprout pushing up is 屯 (difficult birth), and the choice teaches the intent where the deer line is only flavour. In the strip the sprout is a tiny comma until the last frames, so it reads weakly on first sight. 'Always' goes beyond the text: the Judgment promises great success and says to set up helpers. 'Starts are hard. / Get help.' is just as plain and closer to 利建侯.

decision.text:
Starts are
always hard.
decision.why: The sprout straining up through the ground is 屯 (difficult beginnings) exactly.

feedback: Clear and fun: cyan rain falls on the figure, it stops, and the figure settles. 'Wait in the rain; / it will pass.' says what is shown and is the hexagram's intent, and the example short proved it works. The guests line is one line's flavour. Only small gains are left, such as the rain being a little heavier or longer so the waiting registers.

The rain falling on the waiting figure is clear, and the example short already works. The text is about waiting for rain to come (clouds rise to heaven; eat, drink and be at ease while waiting), not waiting out rain. So 'it will pass' reverses the picture slightly. It still teaches patience, which is the intent. 'Wait. / Eat, rest; it comes.' is truer to the text, but the current sentence is acceptable.

decision.text:
Wait in the rain;
it will pass.
decision.why: Waiting out the rain is 需 (waiting); the guests line is one line flavour. The example short showed it works.

feedback: Clear: one figure, a second walks up and stands beside it, and they settle together. 'Choose who you / stand beside' names the action and teaches 比: whom you join, and joining in time. The Renoir lunch was fine, but this is simpler and more active.

Two figures coming to stand together is clear at a glance. 'Choose who you stand beside' matches the Judgment (examine yourself before joining; latecomers fare badly) and line 3 (joining the wrong people). Plain and short. Ship it.

decision.text:
Choose who you
stand beside
decision.why: A second figure walking up to stand beside the first is 比 (holding together).

feedback: Right to keep. The foot-strokes clip is subtle, just 履 being written, and 'Stood on a tiger's tail. Not bitten.' is the hexagram's own Judgment. It is vivid, fun and needs no history. The only thing left is making sure the delivery lands the surprise ('Not bitten.' on its own beat).

Right to keep. The foot being placed is invisible in the strip, and the tiger's tail is the Judgment itself: conduct that is careful and correct survives danger. The sentence spells out who stands on what, and the outcome. It is concrete and fun.

decision.text:
Stood on a tiger's
tail. Not bitten.
decision.why: The foot coming down is subtle in the clip; the tiger tail judgment is the best known image of 履.

feedback: Right to keep. The clip is a flat frame with small yellow bits that lift slightly and does not read as 'together'. 'Parted, they weep. Met, they laugh.' is plain, emotional and teaches fellowship. It loses a point only because it is a line rather than the Judgment's 'fellowship in the open'. No better option is on the table.

Keeping is right: the frame lifting reads as an object lifting, not as people together. 'Parted, they weep. Met, they laugh.' is concrete, and fellowship is the hexagram's own subject, so it teaches intent, not just flavour. A point short of 10 only because line 5 is about finally meeting after struggle rather than the Judgment's open fellowship (in the open field, across the great water).

decision.text:
Parted, they weep.
Met, they laugh.
decision.why: The 同 clip (a frame, the inside lifting) reads weakly as "together"; the line "Parted, they weep. Met, they laugh." is strong.

feedback: The green bug glyphs piling out of the pink bowl are lively and read as 'something breeding in a container'. A newcomer won't know they are worms, but they will see a swarm. 'Plan three days, check three days' needs the Judgment, so the character is the right choice. The weak point is that the sentence names the decay, not the hexagram's intent, which is to repair it. 'What you leave shut / goes bad. Fix it.' or 'Open it up / and fix it' would teach the action.

The drawing is the strongest in the set: worms pouring out of a shut bowl is literally 蠱. The sentence explains how the decay started. The hexagram's point is fixing it (repair what was spoiled, three days before and after). 'What you leave / shut goes bad' warns but teaches no action. 'Open it up / and fix it' or 'Rot left alone / spreads. Fix it' carries the intent and still fits the swarm.

decision.text:
What you leave
shut goes bad
decision.why: Worms swarming out of a shut bowl is the character and the hexagram (decay you must fix) at once.

feedback: The best 3D moment in the set: the tall figure tips forward and three cyan squares light up beneath it. It is fun and legible as 'leaning over something'. 'Lean down to / see what is small' matches the action. The intent of 臨 (the strong drawing near to look after those below, with care) is only half taught, because the squares are not obviously 'small people or things'. Still better than 'Too comfortable? Worry a little.' Something like 'Come close to / those below you' would teach the intent more directly.

The big eye leaning down over three small squares reads clearly and is fun. 臨 is the superior drawing near to the people to teach and care for them (教思無窮，容保民無疆). 'See what is small' leans toward inspection rather than care. 'Lean down to / those below you' or 'Come close / to those you lead' is closer to the intent. The choice over the 'too comfortable' line is right.

decision.text:
Lean down to
see what is small
decision.why: The big eye leaning down to look at small things is 臨 (overseeing, drawing near).

feedback: The pieces falling off the block to leave the base are visible and match 剝. But 'Stripped back / to the base' describes the picture; it is not a lesson. A newcomer gets 'things fall away' and nothing to do about it. The hexagram's advice is to not push while things are being stripped, and to secure the base. 'When it falls apart, / hold the base' or 'Let it fall; / keep the base' would teach. As written it only narrowly beats the bed-legs line, which is vivid.

The clip shows pieces coming off until a base is left, which reads. The sentence describes the picture but teaches nothing, and it inverts the hexagram: in 剝 the base goes first (the bed's legs, then its frame) and only the top line survives. The lesson of the text is not to push forward while things fall (不利有攸往) and to shore up what is below (上以厚下安宅). The current line 'The bed breaks at the legs first' is truer. For the character, use something like 'When it falls apart, / don't push' or 'Shore up / what's below'.

decision.text:
Stripped back
to the base
decision.why: Pieces falling off the block until only the base stands is 剝 (stripping away).

feedback: The clip reads as a character being assembled. The foot walking back and the road drawn after it are not visible as a return. 'The way out is / the way back' is a riddle, the kind of mannered phrase the rules warn against, and it does not say what returns or why. The current 'Midwinter: rest. / The light returns.' is plain, true to the Image and teaches 復 directly. Keep the current lesson, or use the character with 'What left / comes back'.

'The way out is the way back' is a riddle, the mannered prose the brief rules out, and a newcomer can't parse it. The clip mostly looks like 復 being drawn stroke by stroke; the foot walking back isn't clear. The current 'Midwinter: rest. The light returns.' already teaches the intent (return after the low point). If the character is kept, use the key line 1: 'Gone a little wrong? / Turn back.' (不遠復).

decision.text:
The way out is
the way back
decision.why: The foot walking back into the passage is 復 (return).

feedback: The clip is hard to read: a yellow piece glows inside the left part of 頤, and nothing reads as a jaw or as food spilling out. 'Mind what goes in / and what comes out' is true to the Image (care with food and words), but at 8 words it is over the 3-7 limit and abstract. 'Stop staring at / someone's plate.' is plain, funny and teaches self-reliance at first sight. Keep the current lesson, or shorten to 'Mind what goes in / your mouth' only if the spill becomes visible.

The sentence is almost exactly the Image (be careful of words, moderate in eating and drinking, 慎言語，節飲食), and it is plain. The jaw with something rising inside reads reasonably well, though the 'spill out' moment is small in the strip. It is better than the envy line, which is line 1 flavour.

decision.text:
Mind what goes in
and what comes out
decision.why: The open jaw with things spilling out teaches minding what goes in and comes out, which is 頤 (nourishment).

feedback: Good. A glowing moon waxes and wanes between two steady bars, which is easy to follow and pretty to watch, and 'Change shape, / keep your course' names exactly what it shows. The current 'No game in this field. Move.' would confuse a newcomer on a hexagram about persistence. The heart that appears at the end is unexplained but harmless.

The moon waxing and waning between two steady lines is a clear, fun picture of constancy through change, and 'keep your course' matches the Image (stand firm, don't change direction, 立不易方). 'Change shape' is slightly ambiguous: it could read as advice to change yourself. 'Shapes change; / keep your course' would remove that. A good choice over the field-with-no-game line.

decision.text:
Change shape,
keep your course
decision.why: The moon changing shape between two steady lines shows constancy through change; the current line needs context.

feedback: The bright moon shrinking beside 日 is watchable, and 'Keep your light / low and on' teaches the intent. But in the strip the waning reads as a ball getting a little smaller, not as a thin crescent that stays lit, so 'low and on' is only partly shown. 'A prince acted mad to stay alive' is not really history-dependent: it explains itself and is more fun. A close call. The character wins only if the crescent clearly stays lit on screen.

The sentence is accurate and plain: it is the Image's 用晦而明 (dim your light and stay bright). The clip only draws 明 and shows a moon that mostly goes out; the 'dimmed but still lit' state isn't clear in the strip. The Prince Ji line does need history, so the character is still the better option. Make the lit crescent hold long enough to register.

decision.text:
Keep your light
low and on
decision.why: Keeping a light low but on is the hexagram (light hidden in dark times); the prince story needs history. The waning moon is our own story of 明, not its etymology.

feedback: The cyan 角 lifting free of the pink 牛 does read as 'a part comes loose', and 'Cut it loose / and move on' is plain and fits 解 (release). A newcomer will not see an ox horn or a knife, only one half of a sign floating off. That is still better than the thieves line, which is one line's flavour and needs explaining. Making the knife stroke visibly slice before the lift would sell 'cut'.

True to the character: knife, ox and horn, with the horn cut free, and 'Cut it loose and move on' fits the Judgment (release, then return or go early) and the Image (pardon faults). In the strip the horn lifting is small and could read as a stroke being placed, so a newcomer may miss the cut. The sentence is good. The payoff needs to be bigger on screen.

decision.text:
Cut it loose
and move on
decision.why: The horn cut free is 解 (release) in the character itself.

feedback: Clear at first sight: a tree grows and walls close round it, so the final frame is a tree boxed in. The sentence names what is shown, and it beats the dry-lake line, which needs the Image explained. One small mismatch: the tree ends pressed flat, not growing, so 'keep growing' is said over a picture of the tree being stopped. 'Boxed in, / keep growing' or a tree that pushes up once more at the end would make it a 9.

The character is the right choice: walls closing round a tree shows 困 (hemmed in) at a glance, and the dry lake needs explaining. The sentence is close to the Image (a person keeps to their aim under pressure), but the clip ends with the tree pressed flat, so 'keep growing' says the opposite of what the viewer just saw. 'Pressed in, / hold to your aim' or 'Hemmed in, / stand firm' matches both the drawing and the text.

decision.text:
Pressed in,
keep growing
decision.why: The walls pressing the tree flat show 困 (oppression) directly; the lake image needs explaining.

feedback: Keeping the line is right: the strip shows 井 being drawn plus a small cyan blob, and nobody would see water rippling in a well. 'The well is clean. No one drinks.' is plain and odd enough to stick. But it is line 3 (flavour, and a sad exception), not the intent of 井: the well that feeds everyone and does not move. A better clip, or 'The town moves; / the well stays' over a clearer well, would teach more.

The clip is weak, and I agree: it shows 井 plus a cyan ripple and acts out nothing, so keeping the line is defensible. But the kept line teaches an exception, the one sad line in the hexagram. The hexagram's point is in the Judgment: the town changes, the well does not, and it feeds everyone who comes. The better fix is to put the Judgment sentence into the kept slot ('Towns move. / The well stays.') or improve the clip. Keeping line 3 as it is gives flavour, not intent.

decision.text:
The well is clean.
No one drinks.
decision.why: The well clip is the weakest: four beams and a ripple. "The well is clean. No one drinks." is a clear, odd image.

feedback: The clip is modest: legs are drawn, a yellow dot glows between them, and the top piece drops on. A newcomer sees a character assembling and may not see a pot over a fire. 'A steady base lets things cook' is plain but flat. 'The legs break. Duke wears dinner.' is funnier, teaches the same point from the failure side, and needs no context. I would keep the duke line, or make the fire clearly flicker and the bowl clearly land.

The clip is subtle: the fire is a small yellow dot, and the bowl dropping onto the legs reads as the character being assembled. 'A steady base / lets things cook' is plain but vague, and it leans on the legs, which are line 4's image. 鼎's intent is nourishing and setting the new order in its right place (正位凝命). 'Duke wears dinner' is funnier and still shows why the base matters. It is close. A sharper sentence, e.g. 'Set it level, / then cook', would decide it.

decision.text:
A steady base
lets things cook
decision.why: The cauldron set on its legs over a fire shows 鼎 plainly; the duke joke is funny but is about one line.

feedback: The sign turning round and back is a clear, fun action. But what it shows is literally the Judgment's 'stilling the back': it turns its back. 'Stop, and look / at where you are' is plain and fits 艮, though the comma makes it a little stiff. The clip actually illustrates the current line well, so 'Stillness starts / in the back' over this drawing could beat both. As it stands it is a sound choice.

The turning figure that holds still is readable, and the sentence matches the Image: thoughts do not go beyond one's place (思不出其位). It is plain, and a newcomer gets it. 'Stillness starts in the back' is truer to the Judgment's wording but harder to picture. Minor issue: the comma is not needed ('Stop and look / at where you are').

decision.text:
Stop, and look
at where you are
decision.why: The figure turning round to look and holding still teaches stopping; "Stillness starts in the back" is harder to picture.

feedback: The clip is one of the weaker ones: 旅 gets bigger in steps, but no people or flag are legible, so the 'walking toward you' reads as a zoom. 'Travel light; keep moving' is plain but partly invented; the text's point is that the traveller should be modest and careful as a guest. 'The wanderer burns his own inn' is vivid and fun but is one line. I'd take the character only with a sentence nearer the intent, such as 'Far from home, / be a good guest'.

A figure walking closer in hops is readable and fun. 'Travel light' isn't in the text. The Judgment says small success for the wanderer who stays modest and correct, and the Image says don't linger over lawsuits. 'Keep moving' only half fits. The burnt inn is one line but a vivid warning about a guest's conduct. A sentence closer to the intent, e.g. 'Far from home, / walk softly', would earn the character a higher score.

decision.text:
Travel light;
keep moving
decision.why: People walking toward you with a flag is 旅 (travelling); the burnt inn is one line.

feedback: Charming: the two yellow strokes pop up and bob above the open mouth like laughter or raised eyebrows, which is fun at first sight. 'Joy is better / shared out loud' is plain and true to the Image of friends joined in talk. That clearly beats a lesson about one painting.

The laugh-lines bobbing out of the open mouth are clear and fun, and the choice over a single painting's lesson is right. 'Out loud' adds little. The Image is friends joining in talk and practice (朋友講習), so the text's point is shared joy, not loud joy. 'Joy grows / when it's shared' or 'Share your joy / with friends' is plainer and truer.

decision.text:
Joy is better
shared out loud
decision.why: The lines lifting out of an open mouth like laughter is 兌 (joy); the painting lesson is about one painting.

feedback: The sentence is excellent: 'When it is done, / stay awake' is plain and is exactly the intent of 既濟. The clip is weak for a newcomer: one half of 既 twists round and back, and neither the bowl nor 'the meal is done' can be seen, so it reads as a spin. It still beats 'Fine silk turns to rags', which needs explaining. The sentence carries it.

The sentence is right: it is the Image's 思患而豫防之 (after completion, anticipate trouble), in plain words. It is still better than line 4's rags, whose meaning is disputed. Make the turn legible.

decision.text:
When it is done,
stay awake
decision.why: Turning away from the finished meal and staying awake is 既濟 (after completion, stay careful).

feedback: The strip shows a curl growing into 屯. Nothing on screen strains or looks hard, so the sentence has to do all the teaching. 'Starts are hard. Get help.' is plain and covers both halves of the Judgment (hard birth, 利建侯). Dropping 'always' is right. The deer line is more vivid but only one line's image, so choosing the character is reasonable. To score higher, the clip itself would need to show the struggle, e.g. the sprout stalling before it breaks through.

The sentence is true to the Judgment (a hard birth, 勿用有攸往, 利建侯) and dropping 'always' is right. But the strip is a small comma for three frames before the character appears, so nothing on screen shows strain, and all the teaching falls on 'Get help'. It would score higher with a sentence that also carries 'don't push ahead yet', e.g. 'Hard start?\nDon't go alone.'

decision.text:
Starts are hard.
Get help.
decision.why: The sprout drawing is thin, so the sentence has to teach, and this one covers both halves of the Judgment: a hard birth, then set up helpers (利建侯). It also drops 'always', which the text does not say.

feedback: The rain streaks and the figure lying down read clearly, and 'Eat, rest, wait' is the Image's 飲食宴樂. Eat, rest, wait.' or 'Waiting on rain? Eat and rest.', would score higher.

Good choice: the falling rain is the clearest thing in the strip, and 'Eat, rest, wait' is the Image's 飲食宴樂, which is plain and fun. One small mismatch: the Image's clouds have risen but no rain has fallen yet, while the clip shows rain falling, so 'Rain on the way?' goes a little against the screen. 'Rain?\nEat, rest, wait.' would match what the viewer sees.

decision.text:
Rain on the way?
Eat, rest, wait.
decision.why: The cloud and rain are clear on screen, and the figure lying down at the end reads as rest. The Image says clouds rise to heaven and you eat, drink and are at ease while you wait, so this fixes the slight reversal in 'it will pass'.

feedback: This is the strongest pairing. The worms visibly breed and swarm out of the bowl, and 'Found rot? Clean it out.' turns the image into the hexagram's intent (fix the decay) in five plain words. The only thing left to improve would be a closing beat of the swarm being cleared.

The worm swarm is the strongest clip, and 'Found rot? Clean it out.' teaches 幹蠱 (setting the decay right) instead of only warning about it. It is plain, short and true. 'Fix it' might sit a bit closer to 幹 than 'clean it out', but that difference is small.

decision.text:
Found rot?
Clean it out.
decision.why: The worm swarm in the bowl is the strongest drawing in the set. The sentence now teaches what the hexagram asks for, which is fixing the decay, not just a warning that it happens.

feedback: The tall figure tipping down over three small cyan boxes reads as 'big one comes to small ones'. On a phone the lean can also look like the figure falling flat. The clip reads (the tall form tilts over three glowing squares), and the sentence fits 臨's intent and the Image's 教思无窮, 容保民. 'Those below you' sounds a little stiff and hierarchical for a newcomer. decision.text:
Come close to
those below you

Pieces falling away until the base stands is readable. 'Shore up the base' is the Image's 上以厚下安宅 and gives the viewer something to do. It skips the Judgment's 不利有攸往 (don't make a move while things are stripping away), but the Image reading is fair and plain.

decision.text:
Falling apart?
Shore up the base.
decision.why: Pieces fall off until only the base stands, which the Image turns into advice: those above make the base thick to secure the house (上以厚下安宅). It gives the viewer something to do instead of only describing the picture.

feedback: Right call. The strip is 復 drawn stroke by stroke, and no foot or walking back is visible. 'Midwinter: rest. The light returns.' is plain, true to the Image and teaches return. 'The way out is the way back' is a riddle. I would ship it.

Keeping the current lesson is right. The strip shows 復 being written stroke by stroke, with no foot walking back that anyone could see. 'Midwinter: rest. decision.text:
Stop staring at

The moon dims visibly and no crescent can be seen, so 'Dim your light' says what is on screen and is the Image's 用晦而明. It drops the 'but keep it lit' half (明 stays inside). 'Dim' still suggests a light that is on, so this is acceptable. Plain and short.

decision.text:
Dark times?
Dim your light.

feedback: The sentence is good and true to 解. On screen, though, the knife is not readable and the cyan 角 only drifts up a little at the end, so 'cut' has little support in the picture. Hold to your aim.
